stimulus.text:
Saint-Domingue (the French colony on the western part of Hispaniola), about 1791:

| Group | Number |
|---|---|
| Enslaved Africans | about 500,000 |
| Free whites | about 30,000 |
| Free people of mixed race (gens de couleur) | about 30,000 |

Free people of mixed race owned about a third of the enslaved people on the island but were barred from political participation.
stimulus.source_note: Figures as given in Barron's AP U.S. History Premium, 2027, Chapter 5, Topic 3.6.

source: original; stimulus table from figures in Barron's AP U.S. History Premium, 2027, Chapter 5, Topic 3.6.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, C. The Impact of the American Revolution Abroad

stem: The mixed-race planters' position in the table best explains why the revolution in Saint-Domingue unfolded in three phases, because

options.text: Each group rebelled for its own reasons: whites, mixed-race planters, and enslaved people
All three groups agreed from the very start to abolish slavery together
options.misconception: They never agreed; whites defended slavery, mixed-race planters owned enslaved people themselves, and the enslaved rose last, for freedom.

options.text: France granted each group its demands in turn, ending the fighting quickly
options.misconception: France granted nothing in turn; each phase was a rebellion, and the enslaved won freedom by fighting, not by French grant.

options.text: The British army organized the three groups into a single fighting force
options.misconception: Britain never organized them; the phases were separate rebellions by groups with different aims.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the three groups held different stakes — whites who ruled, mixed-race owners barred from politics, and a vast enslaved majority. Each rose when its own grievance peaked, so the revolution came in waves.
rationales.B: Agreement never existed; the mixed-race planters owned a third of the enslaved people, so they did not seek abolition.
rationales.C: France conceded nothing in order; the rebellion's phases were driven by the groups themselves, not by Paris.
rationales.D: No British force united them; the three phases were three separate risings with separate aims.
rationales.general:
1. Sort the table. Background: three groups held three stakes — whites who ruled, mixed-race owners barred from politics, enslaved people in chains.
2. Ask what each wanted. Background: whites wanted looser French rule, mixed-race planters wanted political rights, the enslaved wanted freedom.
3. Stack the risings. Each group rose for its own reason, so the revolution came in three phases, not one.
Remember: one island can hold three revolutions — sort the groups by interest before you sort the events.
